claims.title: Military coercion
claims.statement: Strikes alone rarely achieve maximal Iranian political compliance.
claims.geography: Iran; explicitly declared maximal objectives of each strike campaign
claims.effect: Compliance sustained for 180 days after a campaign
claims.falsifier: A documented maximal demand is fully met for 180 days without occupation.
claims.support: Survival and resistance after major damage
claims.alternative: Negotiations, sanctions, limited military objectives; do not treat delay as failure.
claims.attribution: Report-derived hypothesis; not a verified direct quotation from Pape.
claims.plain: Strikes alone seldom force Iran to meet its attackers' maximum political demands.

claims.title: Maritime denial
claims.geography: Strait of Hormuz; commercial oil passage
claims.effect: At least 10% lower volume than the prior four-quarter mean for 30 days, with corroborated Iranian interference
claims.falsifier: 90 days of normal passage under a documented credible threat and active countermeasures.
claims.alternative: Demand, voluntary rerouting, production cuts and tracking coverage can change flows.
claims.attribution: Report-derived hypothesis; not a verified direct quotation from Pape.

claims.title: Political concessions
claims.statement: Maritime coercion yields durable political concessions.
claims.effect: A substantive policy change sustained for 180 days with documentary attribution to maritime pressure
claims.falsifier: An agreed concession is reversed within 180 days, or a completed negotiation produces none.
claims.support: Documented policy reversal tied to coercion
claims.alternative: Routine diplomacy, unrelated bargains and temporary ceasefires are competing explanations.
claims.attribution: Report-derived hypothesis; not a verified direct quotation from Pape.
claims.approved_by: Owner sign-off of AI proposal (Claude); not expert-reviewed

claims.title: Regional alignment
claims.effect: Two new substantive security or economic agreements favorable to Iran, sustained for 180 days
claims.falsifier: Defense integration against Iran increases with no comparable accommodation.
claims.support: Durable favorable security and economic arrangements
claims.alternative: Hedging can produce both accommodation and balancing; count both.
claims.attribution: Report-derived hypothesis; not a verified direct quotation from Pape.

claims.title: Nuclear trajectory
claims.statement: Attacks increase long-run nuclear reconstitution incentives.
claims.geography: Iranian nuclear policy and verified facilities
claims.effect: Verified rebuilding plus independently documented policy hardening within 24 months
claims.falsifier: Verified capacity reduction and cooperative inspection sustained for 12 months.
claims.alternative: Inspection gaps are uncertainty; technical capacity and political intent are separate.
claims.attribution: Report-derived hypothesis; not a verified direct quotation from Pape.
claims.plain: Attacks give Iran a stronger long-term reason to rebuild its nuclear program.
claims.approved_by: Owner sign-off of AI proposal (Claude); not expert-reviewed

claims.title: Net strategic power
claims.geography: Iran relative to its pre-campaign position
claims.effect: Improvement across military regeneration, real trade and durable diplomatic influence over 24 months
claims.falsifier: Deterioration in at least two dimensions sustained for 12 months.
claims.support: Broad improvement in resilience and bargaining outcomes
claims.alternative: Survival and disruption alone do not show an increase in net power.
claims.attribution: Report-derived hypothesis; not a verified direct quotation from Pape.

assessments.rationale: No preregistered campaign objectives and matched outcomes have yet been assembled. Regime survival cannot resolve this claim. Retrospective, provisional analyst judgment using publications dated before the cutoff; no archived as-of snapshot or human approval.

Limited support: the EIA series shows a substantial decline in estimated oil passage. Attribution and persistence under countermeasures remain unverified, so the evidence does not warrant moderate or stronger support. Retrospective, provisional analyst judgment using publications dated before the cutoff; no archived as-of snapshot or human approval.

No reviewed documentary chain connects maritime pressure to a concession sustained for 180 days. Sanctions show costs, not the absence of all concessions. Insufficient evidence. Retrospective, provisional analyst judgment using publications dated before the cutoff; no archived as-of snapshot or human approval.

Slight challenge: the US security guarantee for Qatar is consistent with external balancing. One state and one agreement cannot establish the regional trend; accommodation may coexist. Retrospective, provisional analyst judgment using publications dated before the cutoff; no archived as-of snapshot or human approval.

Inspection gaps establish uncertainty, not incentives or weaponization. Verified rebuilding and a separate policy-intent measure are still required. Retrospective, provisional analyst judgment using publications dated before the cutoff; no archived as-of snapshot or human approval.

Limited challenge: renewed EU sanctions and the IMF adverse growth assessment show diplomatic and economic costs. Military regeneration and durable influence are not measured, so a stronger judgment is not warranted. Retrospective, provisional analyst judgment using publications dated before the cutoff; no archived as-of snapshot or human approval.

Against this, Iran agreed in June 2026 to down-blend its stockpile under IAEA supervision, though the agreement collapsed (E008). evidence.title: Iran ends the Cairo inspection agreement and makes cooperation conditional on the end of threats
evidence.excerpt: Iran stated that “the conditions resulting from acts of aggression and the continuation of threats have created a situation in which the normal implementation of safeguards is legally untenable and materially impracticable.”
evidence.rationale: Documented policy change on inspections that Iran itself links to the attacks: the Cairo agreement was declared terminated on 20 Nov 2025, and cooperation was made conditional on the end of threats. This bears only on the policy-hardening part of the H5 test. Satellite imagery showed activity at Isfahan, Natanz and Fordow, but the IAEA could not confirm its nature, so no rebuilding is verified.
evidence.confounders: Bargaining leverage before negotiations; physical safety at damaged sites; Iranian concern about information security of inspections.
evidence.missingness: No access to any affected facility; stockpile size and location unknown since June 2025.
evidence.effect: Access to declared facilities and Iranian policy statements on safeguards

evidence.title: IAEA verification stops again after the February 2026 attacks; access only at Bushehr
evidence.excerpt: “On 28 February 2026, the United States of America and Israel launched further military attacks on Iran, including on the sites of some nuclear facilities. Consequently, the Agency stopped conducting verification activities in Iran.”
evidence.rationale: Second loss of access. The only verification in the period was at Bushehr (1–3 June 2026), with Iran’s cooperation. Satellite imagery showed damage at Natanz and severe damage to the Khondab heavy water plant. Damage from attacks is not a verified capacity reduction, and the absence of access does not show rebuilding.
evidence.confounders: Active hostilities and safety limits on inspections.
evidence.missingness: No information on enrichment, centrifuge inventory or stockpile; no access to 21 of 22 declared facilities.
evidence.effect: Verification access and reported damage to nuclear sites

evidence.title: Short-lived US–Iran memorandum on down-blending; IAEA has no access for more than a year
evidence.excerpt: Under the 17 June 2026 memorandum both parties agreed to “resolve the disposition of stockpiled enriched material… with the minimum methodology to be down-blended on site under the supervision of the IAEA”.
evidence.rationale: Iran’s signed agreement to down-blend its stockpile under IAEA supervision is evidence against policy hardening. The challenge is weak: the IAEA quotes the memorandum from press sources, no down-blending took place, and both sides declared the memorandum over in July 2026 (it expired on 17 Aug 2026). The report also states that continuity of knowledge over the LEU and 60% HEU has been lost for more than a year, which is uncertainty, not rebuilding.
evidence.confounders: Ceasefire bargaining; the memorandum may reflect pressure, not a change in long-run incentives.
evidence.missingness: Memorandum text is from press reports, not an official release. No in-field verification at any declared facility in the period. Iran disputes the report (INFCIRC/1416, not recorded).
evidence.effect: Iranian commitments on the enriched-uranium stockpile; verification access

evidence.title: Iran rules out verification beyond its safeguards agreement, now or after the war
evidence.publisher: Permanent Mission of Iran to the IAEA (circulated by the IAEA)
evidence.reliability: Primary statement of Iran’s official position; self-interested source
evidence.excerpt: “any verification activities related to the issues beyond Iran’s safeguards commitments have no legal base, and therefore would not be allowed either now or after the termination of war condition.”
evidence.rationale: Iran’s own formal statement that it will refuse verification beyond its basic safeguards agreement even after the war, and that loss of continuity of knowledge is “a natural aftermath of the war”. This is documented policy hardening that Iran links to the attacks, from a source independent of the IAEA reports. It is not evidence of rebuilding, and Iran also says access to safeguarded facilities will return when threats end (paragraph 29).
evidence.confounders: Negotiating position ahead of a possible deal; legal dispute over the reimposed Security Council resolutions.
evidence.missingness: States intentions only; no information on facilities or material.
evidence.license: Short excerpt with attribution; original document linked.
evidence.effect: Iran’s stated policy on IAEA verification

evidence.title: US–Iran memorandum trades Hormuz passage for US commitments; it collapses within weeks
evidence.publisher: Al Jazeera (text read out by a US official)
evidence.document: Explainer, 18 Jun 2026, quoting the 17 Jun 2026 memorandum; collapse dates from GOV/2026/50 paragraph 19 (E008)
evidence.reliability: Major news outlet quoting a US official read-out; no official text published; Iran did not confirm the US version
evidence.excerpt: Iran will make “best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels with no charge for 60 days only”; the US “undertakes to terminate all types of sanctions against Iran in an agreed-upon schedule as part of the final deal” and to end its naval blockade within 30 days.
evidence.rationale: The closest case yet of concessions linked to maritime leverage: US commitments on the blockade, sanctions and a reconstruction plan in exchange for, among other things, Hormuz passage. But the concessions were promises tied to a final deal that never came; the US President called the memorandum “over” on 8 July 2026 and it expired on 17 August 2026. A concession reversed within 180 days matches the H3 falsifier, so this is a potential challenge to the durable-concession claim, not support.
evidence.confounders: The memorandum ended a wider war, so its terms cannot be attributed to maritime pressure alone; the reasons for the collapse are disputed by both sides.
evidence.missingness: No official text; the full 14 points were not published; whether the blockade removal began is not confirmed.
evidence.license: Short excerpt with attribution; original article linked.
evidence.effect: Terms and duration of a US–Iran agreement involving Hormuz passage
evidence.retrieval_note: Page bytes hashed on retrieval; news pages change, so the hash records this copy only.

gaps.name: AIS transit coverage
gaps.detail: Daily IMF PortWatch ship counts are shown but not scored. The total number of ships is not known, and AIS misses ships with transponders switched off. EIA states that Hormuz AIS data have been especially unreliable since the end of February 2026.

gaps.name: War-risk insurance
gaps.detail: No licensed insurance-price data. Missing prices are not estimated.

gaps.name: Nuclear verification
gaps.detail: IAEA reports to 1 September 2026 are recorded (E006–E008). The IAEA has had no access to the stockpile or the enrichment sites since June 2025; the size and location of the enriched uranium are unknown. Later reports are not included.

gaps.name: Diplomatic concessions
gaps.detail: No lasting concession credited to Iranian pressure has been entered. No record does not mean no concession.

gaps.name: Regional / net power
gaps.detail: Treaty, trade, budget and military-rebuilding data still need to be collected and checked.

gaps.name: Iran economy and oil price
gaps.detail: Brent price, the open-market rial rate and annual inflation are shown as context, not scored. The rial rate comes from an unofficial market-data site. Annual inflation is published with a delay of months.
